lessons.title: Density, states of matter and changes of state
lessons.summary: Use the particle model to explain the differences between solids, liquids and gases, calculate density with ρ = m/V, measure density in the lab, and describe what happens to mass during a change of state.
objectives: I can calculate density, mass or volume using ρ = m/V with the correct units.
I can describe how particles are arranged and move in solids, liquids and gases.
I can describe how to measure the density of a regular solid, an irregular solid and a liquid.
I can explain why mass is conserved when a substance changes state.
I can explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change.

activities.title: The particle model of the three states
activities.content:
## Solids, liquids and gases

The **particle model** says that all matter is made of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are constantly moving. The state of a substance depends on how those particles are arranged and how much energy they have.

| | Solid | Liquid | Gas |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Arrangement** | Regular pattern, tightly packed, touching | Random, still close together and touching | Random, far apart |
| **Movement** | Vibrate about fixed positions | Move around each other, slide past | Move freely and fast in all directions |
| **Forces between particles** | Strong | Fairly strong | Very weak |
| **Shape and volume** | Fixed shape, fixed volume | Takes shape of container, fixed volume | Fills the container |
| **Density** | Highest | Slightly lower | Much lower |

A few important details:
- In a solid the particles cannot swap places, which is why a solid keeps its shape.
- Liquids and gases can **flow** because their particles can move past each other.
- Gases can be **compressed** because there is a lot of empty space between the particles. Solids and liquids cannot be squashed much because their particles are already touching.

Density is high when a lot of mass is packed into a small volume. The same particles spread far apart in a gas give a much lower density: steam is about 1600 times less dense than liquid water.

question.text: Match each state of matter to the description of its particles.
question.hint: Think about how much freedom the particles have.
question.explanation: Solids: regular arrangement, vibrating in fixed positions. Liquids: close together but able to move past each other. Gases: far apart and moving freely.

pairs.right: Regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions
Close together, random, able to slide past each other
Far apart, moving quickly in random directions

activities.title: Density
activities.content:
## What density measures

**Density** tells you how much mass is packed into each unit of volume:

$\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$

- $\rho$ (rho) = density in **kg/m³** (or g/cm³)
- $m$ = mass in **kg** (or g)
- $V$ = volume in **m³** (or cm³)

Water has a density of **1000 kg/m³**, which is the same as **1 g/cm³**. Anything less dense than this floats on water; anything denser sinks.

**Unit conversions you must be able to do**
- 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³
- 1 kg = 1000 g
- To convert **g/cm³ to kg/m³**, multiply by **1000**. (Iron is 7.9 g/cm³ = 7900 kg/m³.)

**Rearranging**
- $m = \rho V$
- $V = \dfrac{m}{\rho}$

Use the triangle with $m$ on top and $\rho$ and $V$ underneath.

The particle model explains density differences: a dense material either has heavy particles, or has its particles packed very closely, or both. Lead is denser than aluminium mainly because lead atoms are much heavier.

activities.title: Worked example: density calculations
activities.content:
**1. A block of aluminium has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. What is its density?**

$\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{540}{200} = $ **2.7 g/cm³** = **2700 kg/m³**

**2. A gold bar has a density of 19 300 kg/m³ and a volume of 0.0005 m³. What is its mass?**

$m = \rho V = 19\,300 \times 0.0005 = $ **9.65 kg**

**3. Oil has a density of 920 kg/m³. What volume does 2.3 kg of oil occupy?**

$V = \dfrac{m}{\rho} = \dfrac{2.3}{920} = $ **0.0025 m³** (that is 2.5 litres)

**Watch the units.** If the mass is in grams and the volume in cm³, the density comes out in g/cm³. If they are in kg and m³, the density is in kg/m³. Mixing them up gives an answer that is wrong by a factor of 1000. Write the units next to every number as you work.

question.text: A stone has a mass of 150 g and a volume of 60 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
A steel beam has a density of 7800 kg/m³. Its dimensions are 2 m × 0.1 m × 0.05 m. Calculate the mass of the beam in kg.
question.hint: Find the volume first by multiplying the three lengths, then m = ρV.

activities.title: Required practical: measuring density
activities.content:
## Three methods

**1. A regular solid (e.g. a metal cuboid)**
- Measure the mass on a **balance**.
- Measure length, width and height with a **ruler** or vernier callipers.
- Volume = length × width × height.
- Density = mass ÷ volume.

**2. An irregular solid (e.g. a pebble)**
- Measure the mass on a balance.
- Find the volume by **displacement**: fill a **displacement (eureka) can** with water up to the spout, lower the object in gently, and collect the water that overflows in a **measuring cylinder**. The volume of water pushed out equals the volume of the object.
- Alternatively, note the reading in a measuring cylinder, add the object, and subtract to find the rise.
- Density = mass ÷ volume.

**3. A liquid**
- Put an empty measuring cylinder on the balance and **zero** it (or record its mass).
- Pour in a known volume of liquid, e.g. 50 cm³.
- Read the mass of the liquid, then density = mass ÷ volume.

**Reducing errors**
- Read the measuring cylinder at eye level, from the bottom of the **meniscus**.
- Make sure the object is fully submerged and no water splashes out.
- Repeat and calculate a mean.
- For small objects, measure several together and divide, because a small volume is hard to read accurately.

question.text: Put the steps in order to find the density of an irregularly shaped key.
question.hint: You need both mass and volume before you can divide.
question.explanation: Weigh the key, fill the displacement can to the spout, lower the key in, measure the displaced water volume, then divide mass by volume.
order: Measure the mass of the key on a balance
Fill a displacement can with water up to the spout
Lower the key into the can and collect the water that overflows
Read the volume of displaced water in a measuring cylinder
Divide the mass by the volume to find the density

activities.title: Changes of state
activities.content:
## Changing state

Heating or cooling a substance can change its state. Each change has a name:

| Change | Name |
|---|---|
| Solid → liquid | **Melting** |
| Liquid → gas | **Boiling** (or evaporating at the surface) |
| Gas → liquid | **Condensing** |
| Liquid → solid | **Freezing** |
| Solid → gas directly | **Sublimating** |

**Mass is conserved.** When ice melts, the water has exactly the same mass as the ice did. The particles are the same; only their arrangement and movement have changed. Nothing is created or destroyed. If you boil water in a sealed container, the steam has the same mass as the water it came from.

**Changes of state are physical changes.** The substance is still the same substance, and if you reverse the heating or cooling, it changes back with the same properties. Ice, water and steam are all H₂O.

A **chemical change** is different: new substances are formed and the change is usually hard to reverse. Burning wood is a chemical change. Melting wax is a physical change.

**Volume can change even though mass does not.** Most substances expand when they melt, and expand hugely when they boil, so their density falls. Water is unusual: ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why it floats.

question.text: True or false: when 50 g of ice melts, the mass of the water formed is less than 50 g because some particles are lost.
question.hint: Do any particles disappear when the arrangement changes?
question.explanation: False. A change of state is a physical change in which no particles are lost or created, so the mass stays at exactly 50 g.

question.text: Which is the best particle-model explanation of why a gas is much less dense than a liquid of the same substance?
question.hint: Same particles, same mass each, so what is different?
question.explanation: The particles are the same, but in a gas they are much further apart, so the same mass occupies a much larger volume, giving a lower density.

options.text: The gas particles are much further apart, so the same mass takes up a much larger volume
The gas particles are lighter than the liquid particles
options.feedback: The particles are identical; only their spacing changes.

options.text: Some particles are destroyed when the liquid boils
options.feedback: Mass is conserved during a change of state.

question.text:
A student wants to find the density of a small irregular metal ornament.

(a) Describe a method the student could use, naming the equipment needed. (3 marks)

(b) The ornament has a mass of 216 g and a volume of 80 cm³. Calculate its density. (2 marks)
question.hint: Irregular shape means you cannot use a ruler for volume. Think about displacing water.
question.explanation: (a) Measure the mass with a balance. Fill a displacement can to the spout (or part-fill a measuring cylinder and note the reading). Lower the ornament in and measure the volume of water displaced with a measuring cylinder. Density = mass ÷ volume. (b) ρ = 216 ÷ 80 = 2.7 g/cm³.

markScheme.criterion: Measure the mass using a balance / scales
Find the volume by displacement of water (eureka can or measuring cylinder)
Calculate density by dividing mass by volume

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Solids**: regular, tightly packed, vibrate in place. **Liquids**: close, random, slide past each other. **Gases**: far apart, fast, random.
- $\rho = m / V$. Units: kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Water is 1000 kg/m³.
- Regular solid: ruler and balance. Irregular solid: balance and **displacement**. Liquid: measuring cylinder on a zeroed balance.
- Changes of state (melting, boiling, condensing, freezing, sublimating) are **physical** changes: **mass is conserved** and the change can be reversed.
- Gases are much less dense because their particles are far apart, not because the particles are lighter.

practiceQuestions.text: A block has a mass of 800 g and a volume of 400 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
Convert a density of 0.8 g/cm³ into kg/m³.
Copper has a density of 8900 kg/m³. Calculate the mass of 0.002 m³ of copper.
A sample of liquid has a mass of 45 g and a density of 0.9 g/cm³. Calculate its volume.
A measuring cylinder contains 40 cm³ of water. When a pebble of mass 108 g is added, the level rises to 76 cm³. Calculate the density of the pebble in g/cm³.
practiceQuestions.hint: The volume of the pebble is the rise in water level.

practiceQuestions.text: Which change of state is a gas turning into a liquid?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think of water droplets forming on a cold window.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Condensing is gas to liquid. Boiling is the reverse. Freezing is liquid to solid, melting is solid to liquid.

metadata.blanksText: A change of state is a ___ change, and the ___ of the substance stays the same before and after.

practiceQuestions.hint: It is not a chemical change; and one measurable quantity is conserved.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Changes of state are physical changes; mass is conserved.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO statements about gases are explained by the particle model?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the spacing of gas particles.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gas particles are far apart, so a gas can be compressed and has a low density. Gases do not have a fixed shape, and their particles move quickly, not slowly.

options.text: Gases can be compressed because there is a lot of space between the particles
Gases have a low density because the particles are spread far apart
Gases keep a fixed shape because the particles are in fixed positions

practiceQuestions.text: A student measures the density of a liquid using a measuring cylinder and a balance. Describe two things the student should do to make the measurements as accurate as possible.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how you read a measuring cylinder and how you deal with the mass of the empty cylinder.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Read the volume at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus, and zero the balance with the empty cylinder on it (or subtract the mass of the empty cylinder). Using a larger volume and repeating readings also improves accuracy.

markScheme.criterion: Read the measuring cylinder at eye level / bottom of the meniscus
Zero / tare the balance with the empty cylinder, or subtract the mass of the empty cylinder, or use a large volume / repeat

practiceQuestions.text:
A sealed flask contains 0.5 kg of water. The flask is heated until all the water has turned to steam.

(a) State the mass of steam in the flask and explain your answer using the particle model. (2 marks)

(b) Explain, in terms of particles, why the steam has a much lower density than the water. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: No particles can escape a sealed flask. Density depends on how closely the particles are packed.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) 0.5 kg. The same particles are present; boiling only changes their arrangement and movement, so mass is conserved. (b) In steam the particles are much further apart than in liquid water, so the same mass takes up a far larger volume and the density is lower.

markScheme.criterion: Same number of particles / no particles lost, so mass is conserved
Particles in steam are much further apart / more spread out
Same mass in a larger volume gives a lower density
